html:
An early Thai kingdom in the upper Chao Phraya valley, founded around 1238 and absorbed by Ayutthaya in 1438. The map shows it under this spelling in 1100, before its real founding; at that time the area was held by Khmer outposts and small Mon and Tai towns.

Around 1238 two Tai chiefs, one of them Si Inthrathit, drove out the Khmer governor of Sukhothai, and Si Inthrathit became its first king. His son Ramkhamhaeng, who ruled from about 1279 to 1298, spread its power widely. An inscription dated 1292, the Ramkhamhaeng stele, credits him with creating the Thai script, though some scholars question its age.

Sukhothai took up Theravada Buddhism from monks trained in the Sri Lankan tradition. Its builders made temples with lotus bud towers and its sculptors the graceful walking Buddha. After Ramkhamhaeng the kingdom shrank. Ayutthaya made it a vassal in 1378 and absorbed it in 1438. Thais later looked back on it as the first Thai kingdom, the start of the line told under Sukhothai and Ayutthaya.
